“There’s something unspoken and impossible to explain about [Paweł] Pawlikowski’s cinema,” says French-Polish actor @nadiatereszkiewicz, “something overwhelming that I really admire.” ⁠
⁠
For the Autumn/Winter 2026 issue of AnOther Magazine, Tereszkiewicz, who has appeared in dramas including Stéphanie Di Giusto’s Rosalie, François Ozon’s The Crime Is Mine, and Valeria Bruni Tedeschi’s Forever Young, tells @rose_dodd about her appreciation for Pawlikowski’s postwar trilogy – Ida, Cold War and Fatherland. “I say trilogy, but [they] are not linked directly so much as symbolically.” ⁠
⁠
She says Ida and Cold War speak to her Polish heritage (her grandfather moved to France from Kraków), and Fatherland to her love of Thomas Mann’s writing. In the latter, Mann’s daughter is played by AnOther cover star Sandra Hüller – her force, Tereszkiewicz says, “is truly outstanding”.⁠

💳 An ultra-rare piece of fashion history: The Alexander McQueen x American Express Centurion Card (2004).

In September 2004, American Express celebrated the fifth anniversary of its legendary “Black Card” by collaborating with fashion’s ultimate visionary, Alexander McQueen.

The exclusive, limited-edition card was offered to just 500 of the world’s most elite Centurion members. True to his provocative and conceptual genius, McQueen transformed the card into a piece of art by featuring a stark X-ray image of a model’s leg wearing one of his iconic crystal-embellished, thigh-high stiletto boots.

To commemorate the launch, AMEX hosted an intimate, one-night-only retrospective event in London. The evening featured a curated showcase of 40 archival McQueen runway looks, a live performance by Kate Moss, and a high-profile charity auction. 

Today, the card remains one of the most coveted and elusive artifacts of early-2000s luxury pop culture.

Trainspotting (1996)

Directed by Danny Boyle and based on Irvine Welsh’s 1993 novel, Trainspotting is a British black comedy drama set in Edinburgh, following a group of young men struggling with heroin addiction, unemployment and life on the margins of society. Starring Ewan McGregor, the film became one of the defining works of 1990s British cinema, known for its raw portrayal of addiction, dark humour and rebellious attitude. 

Its unconventional editing, surreal sequences and iconic soundtrack, featuring artists such as Iggy Pop, Underworld and Lou Reed, helped turn it into a cult classic. The film also sparked controversy for its unflinching depiction of drug use, while being praised for capturing the alienation and disillusionment of an entire generation.

Founded in 1963 in a former industrial loft at 231 East 47th Street in Manhattan, became one of the most legendary meeting places of New York’s underground scene. Its walls were covered in silver paint and aluminium foil, giving it the name “Silver Factory”. It functioned as Warhol’s art studio, experimental film set and social hub, attracting artists, musicians, drag performers, socialites and outsiders.

Warhol surrounded himself with a group he called his “Superstars”, including Edie Sedgwick, Nico, Candy Darling, Ultra Violet and Viva. They appeared in his experimental films, attended parties and became part of the Factory’s carefully constructed world of fame and performance. In 1966, Warhol collaborated with The Velvet Underground on the Exploding Plastic Inevitable, an experimental multimedia show combining live music, film projections, strobe lights and performance art. One of his best-known films from this period was Chelsea Girls (1966).

But behind the glamour, the Factory was also surrounded by controversy. Warhol was often accused of exploiting the people around him, turning their private lives, addictions and personal struggles into material for his art while offering little financial compensation. Edie Sedgwick’s turbulent relationship with Warhol remains one of the most discussed examples of this dynamic.

On June 3, 1968, Valerie Solanas, a writer who had previously been associated with the Factory, shot Warhol at his new studio near Union Square. He survived after emergency surgery, but the attack profoundly changed his life and marked the end of the Factory’s original open-door era.

The Factory remains a defining symbol of 1960s New York: a place where art, celebrity, underground culture, sexuality and self-destruction collided.

Hustler White is a satirical black comedy and romance film written and directed by Rick Castro and Bruce LaBruce. Regarded as a cult classic of the 1990s New Queer Cinema movement, the film offers an outrageously provocative and kinky reimagining of Billy Wilder’s classic film noir Sunset Boulevard.

Critics and film historians have often praised the way it combines a fictional romance with an almost documentary-like exploration of the underground subcultures of West Hollywood.

Rick James – Super Freak (1981)

Originally added almost as an afterthought to his album Street Songs, “Super Freak” became one of Rick James’ most recognisable hits. 

Blending funk with playful New Wave influences, its distinctive bassline, exaggerated vocals and provocative lyrics made it an instant classic. 

Released in 1981, the track later became even more influential through MC Hammer’s 1990 hit “U Can’t Touch This”, which famously sampled its iconic bassline.

Sylvain Chomet, the animator behind Dior’s holiday campaign ‘Christian Dior’s Night in Color’, is embroiled in a PR crisis around his alleged use of AI. In an interview with Variety, he defended his work and denied the accusations, which he described as an “attack.”

“The entire creative process is exactly the same as when I started making animated films,” Chomet told Variety, “what has changed is the technology.”

Likely the new technology he is referring to is the automated “interpolation” which he admits to using for Dior’s Ad.

Chomet also went on to address the various hands which had too many fingers, claiming that such errors are an inevitability of hand-drawn animation.

“In that kind of drawing,” he said, “you might see six or seven fingers because you’re trying to convey movement.”

But netizens were not placated by the interview, and discussion around Chomet’s and Dior’s integrity has only appeared to heat up. 

“Bitch it took us five months and seven animators to complete 30 SECONDS OF ANIMATION for the Annecy festival openings be so for fucking real,” one animator posted on X.

And, new problematic details of the film are coming to light, like when a pom-pom sleeping cap suddenly has multiple pom-poms for no logical reason.

“This is not a motion smear,” says one X user, “this is an AI artifact.”

Comparisons to Prada’s recent cartoon ad by John Pomeroy continue to surface as well, with one animator, Ben Wild, claiming on LinkedIn that Dior’s ad was rushed to keep up. 

“It was a rush job,” he said, “the crew were tasked with creating something as they heard Prada was working with an animation legend.” 

Wild also claimed that Dior may pull the ad and release a statement. While his claims are formally unsubstantiated, the post cites “two [unnamed] people who actually worked on the film.”

There is still a great deal of confusion, with Chomet and others involved in the film running defense, while a disappointed audience is voicing their growing distrust. The conversation underscores the increasingly blurred line between digital technology and AI, as well as the increasingly distinct line between acceptable and abhorrent media.

Russell Brand has now been sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison, for one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.
 
In a victim impact statement read by the prosecution’s lead barrister Riel Karmy-Jones KC, the woman he is convicted of raping shared the severe impact it had on her wellbeing, career and intimate relationships.
 
‘It’s something I carry with me every day and it often feels never-ending,’ she said. ‘I doubt my ability to make good decisions and no longer trust my instinct in the way I did.’
 
Another of Brand’s victims, who appeared in person from behind a curtain, spoke of the pain of seeing him celebrated in the media throughout his career. ‘For many years, as his star was rising it was impossible to escape seeing him all over the media, being celebrated for his disgusting behaviour against women like it was all a joke,’ she said, noting it made her feel ‘physically sick… parading around think he can get away with anything’.
 
Brand reportedly did not react in court, but his wife Laura Gallacher was seen shaking her head.

Forecast: frosty, with a side of fabulous.

William Cotterill said he’s had “fantastic harvests” this year on his “fade farm.”

Cotterill is part of a group of savvy sellers speeding up the appearance of patina themselves to meet the demand for distressed vintage garments. Over the summer, he tended to a crop of T-shirts, jackets and hats in a field about a half-hour from his shop, Milennial Vintage in Stockport, England. He hoses down the garments with salt water and and dries them in the sun. He repeats this process twice a week for six weeks, then dismounts the garments from their posts once they’ve achieved a satisfactory level of discoloration.

As some shoppers have grown tired of corporate fast fashion, they’ve become enthralled with tattered, moth-eaten and sun-bleached garments that show traces of the original owner’s habits and lifestyle. But in the discerning world of vintage — where many are concerned about what counts as "true vintage" — fade farming can be a controversial practice. Read more about fade farms at the link in our bio. Visuals by @owenrichards

After independence and Partition in 1947, Punjab needed a new capital to replace Lahore, which had become part of Pakistan. For Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru, Chandigarh was an opportunity to build a city that reflected India’s ambitions for the future. 

In 1950, Nehru invited Swiss-French architect Le Corbusier, one of the most influential figures in modern architecture, to help turn that vision into a plan. 

Le Corbusier and his team organised Chandigarh into sectors, with designated areas for housing, commerce, and government, connected by roads and green spaces. Its design reflected Le Corbusier’s signature focus on natural light, open space, and greenery. 

Chandigarh is often considered Le Corbusier’s greatest work, but building it was far from easy. The heat and monsoon rains required careful planning to keep buildings cool and prevent flooding. He also frequently disagreed with local planners and builders, leading to compromises throughout the decade of construction. 

Chandigarh has grown far beyond its original plan and is now home to more than a million people. Its Capitol Complex is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, but parts of the city face problems with ageing buildings, poor maintenance, and litter. However, Nehru’s vision is still visible in its wide avenues, open spaces, and greenery.
